items.title: Armed Naxals wiped out, must identify, defeat 'dimagi' Naxals: PM in Bastar
items.where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Express News Service)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Linkages between development and spread of extremism; role of external state and non-state actors in internal security · GS3 › Security forces and agencies and their mandate · GS2 › Welfare of vulnerable sections (tribal areas) · GS4 › Inclusive and good governance
items.summary: Celebrating Diwali with the CRPF in Bastar, the PM said armed Naxalites have vanished from the forests but 'intellectual' Naxals remain; only seven districts were categorised as LWE-affected in a February 2026 review.
evolution: Feb 2026
MHA review: only seven districts (five in Chhattisgarh, one each in Jharkhand and Odisha) categorised as LWE-affected.
Home Minister tells the Lok Sabha the country has become 'Naxal-free', against a March 31 target.
PM in Bastar: first Diwali 'when every district of the country is free from Naxalism'.
ideas: From security problem to near-elimination: LWE-affected districts shrank from nearly 200 in the early 2000s to 38 by end-2025 and seven in February 2026; incidents and deaths fell by over four-fifths since 2010.
GS3 · Internal security / LWE
LWE has shrunk from nearly 200 districts to seven, showing that sustained state action can roll back insurgency.
Two-pronged strategy: security forces given the 'freedom to take every necessary decision', paired with development: roads, mobile towers, Eklavya schools and ITIs in affected areas.
GS3 · Linkages between development and extremism
The fall of LWE rests on two legs: firm security operations and the arrival of roads, towers and schools in the forest.

Restoring the state's reach: in affected areas 'life would come to a standstill after sunset' and Naxalites 'snatched away the people's right to vote'; their removal restores citizenship, not just order.
GS3 · LWE / GS2 · Democracy at the grassroots
Ending LWE restores the right to vote and move freely: security here is a precondition for democracy.

The ideological front: the PM said 'intellectual (dimagi) Naxalites' have infiltrated parties and organisations and are 'provoking people against the Constitution'; the battle shifts from forests to ideas.
GS3 · Role of non-state actors / ideology
With armed cadres defeated, the contest over LWE moves to ideas, where the state must win trust, not just territory.
Sacrifice and cost: 76 CRPF personnel were killed in Dantewada in 2010; for the first time in 47 years, no CRPF jawan lost his life on duty over the past year.
GS3 · Security forces / GS4 · Public service values
Not one CRPF jawan killed on duty in a year, a first in 47 years, shows how far the LWE theatre has changed.
keywords: Clearing an area of insurgents, holding it with forces, then building roads, schools and services
LWE's decline follows clear, hold, build: security first, then roads, towers and schools to hold the gains.
The absence of state services that extremists exploit
LWE grew where the state was absent; filling the governance deficit is the lasting cure.
Sympathy or support for LWE ideology among urban groups, distinct from armed cadres
The debate on 'urban Naxals' shows the line the state must hold between countering extremism and protecting dissent.
Roads and mobile towers reaching remote forest villages
Mobile towers in Bastar are last-mile connectivity that also serves as last-mile security.
data: LWE-affected districts: early 2000s, end of 2025, MHA review of February 2026
Government data cited by The Indian Express
LWE-affected districts fell from about 200 in the early 2000s to just seven in February 2026.
Fall in LWE-related incidents and resultant deaths since 2010
Government data cited by The Indian Express
LWE incidents and deaths have fallen by over four-fifths since 2010.
examples: Dantewada, 2010
76 CRPF personnel killed in a single encounter with Naxalites
GS3 · LWE as a security threat
The killing of 76 CRPF personnel in Dantewada in 2010 marked the peak of the LWE threat.
Eklavya schools and ITIs in LWE areas
Education and skilling as part of the counter-LWE strategy
GS4
GS3 · Development and extremism · GS4 · Inclusive governance
Eklavya schools and ITIs in Bastar show inclusive governance: the state wins tribal youth with classrooms, not only guns.
Mobile towers and roads in the forest
Connectivity extended to remote villages after operations
GS3 · Infrastructure for security
Roads and mobile towers in former Naxal areas turn military gains into lasting state presence.
pyqs: Determinants of LWE in eastern India.
Does tribal development policy reflect equity-based governance?
Threats from external state and non-state actors.

trend.t: LWE questions moved from causes (non-implementation of the Fifth Schedule, 2013; determinants in eastern India, 2020) to LWE as a development issue (2022) and then to the government's elimination target and measures (2025). Tribal development reappeared in 2026 as a question of equity-based governance.
trend.watch: LWE has been asked in 2013, 2020, 2022 and 2025, and the 2025 question was about the elimination target itself, so the 'after Naxalism' phase is the next likely angle: consolidation, development and rehabilitation in freed areas.
focus: Security plus development strategy and its results
Fifth Schedule, PESA and Forest Rights Act in freed areas
Rehabilitation of surrendered cadres and victims
Ideological contest: countering extremism while protecting dissent

potential: "Defeating armed insurgency is only half the task; winning the trust of the people is the other half." Discuss with reference to Left Wing Extremism in India. (15 marks)
Examine the role of infrastructure and welfare delivery in containing Left Wing Extremism. (10 marks)
What should be India's strategy to consolidate peace in areas freed from Left Wing Extremism? (15 marks)

practice.q: "Defeating armed insurgency is only half the task; winning the trust of the people is the other half." Discuss with reference to Left Wing Extremism in India.
parts: How the armed threat was defeated
Why trust is the other half

answer.t: LWE-affected districts fell from nearly 200 in the early 2000s to seven in February 2026, yet the PM warned in Bastar that the ideological danger 'has not completely disappeared'.

answer.h: How the armed threat was defeated

pts.t: Security forces were given the freedom to take every necessary decision, with sustained operations in core areas.
pts.ex: No CRPF jawan lost his life on duty over the past year, a first in 47 years.

pts.t: Support that LWE received from sympathisers within the system was targeted alongside armed cadres.
pts.ex: The PM's reference to stopping support from 'people sitting within the system'.

pts.t: Roads and mobile towers opened up the forests to forces and to the state.
pts.ex: Mobile towers and roads in Bastar.

pts.t: Eklavya schools and ITIs brought services into areas once cut off.
pts.ex: Eklavya model residential schools in tribal districts.

pts.t: Joint operations and shared intelligence across the Red Corridor states.
pts.ex: The MHA's periodic district-wise review of LWE affected areas.

pts.t: A time-bound goal created focus and accountability.
pts.ex: The March 31, 2026 'Naxal-free' target announced in the Lok Sabha.

answer.h: Why trust is the other half

pts.t: LWE grew from land alienation, displacement and a governance deficit; these do not end with operations.
pts.ex: Non-implementation of the Fifth Schedule was asked by UPSC in 2013.

pts.t: Unsettled forest rights and displacement for mining can revive grievance.
pts.ex: Forest Rights Act and PESA implementation gaps.

pts.t: Naxalites 'snatched away the right to vote'; elections and gram sabhas must now carry people's voice.
pts.ex: Strong turnout in former LWE areas as a test of trust.

pts.t: An ideology is countered by delivering justice and opportunity, not by force alone.
pts.ex: The PM's call to 'identify' intellectual Naxals.

pts.t: Countering extremist ideology must not chill legitimate criticism and tribal rights activism.
Surrendered cadres and victims need livelihoods, or the cycle restarts.
Shift from security camps to schools, health centres and banks in freed areas.
pts.ex: ITIs and Eklavya schools in Bastar.

pts.t: Implement PESA and the Forest Rights Act in letter and spirit.
pts.ex: Gram sabha consent for land and forest use.

pts.t: Skilling and local jobs to absorb young people.
Community policing and grievance redress to build confidence.
pts.ex: Civic action programmes of the CAPFs.

pts.t: Tribal languages and culture respected in schools and administration.
Keep the district-wise review going to prevent a relapse.

answer.t: The guns have largely fallen silent; India now has to make the state as present in a Bastar village's daily life as the security camp once was.

items.title: The Centre-state divide in food safety regulation
items.syllabus: GS2 › Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; issues in the federal structure · GS2 › Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies · GS2 › Issues relating to health · GS4 › Good governance
items.summary: Maharashtra has gone to the Bombay High Court alleging that the national regulator FSSAI created a parallel enforcement mechanism and encroached on the state's powers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
ideas: The law's design: the 2006 Act gives enforcement to state Commissioners of Food Safety, who appoint Food Safety Officers (FSOs); FSSAI licenses large and inter-state businesses.
GS2 · Statutory bodies / federal structure
The 2006 Act makes the state Commissioner the enforcer; FSSAI's role is to set standards and license big players.

Parallel enforcement: a May 2023 FSSAI order said centrally licensed premises would be inspected by 'central food safety officers', even when a complaint reaches the state; states say the Act has no provision for central FSOs.
GS2 · Centre–state friction in regulation
Maharashtra's plea shows how a regulator's executive order can quietly redraw the federal division of work.
Expanding central jurisdiction: five-star hotels, all e-commerce platforms, nutraceuticals and 'proprietary foods' have been brought under central licensing.
GS2 · Regulatory overreach
Bringing e-commerce and proprietary foods under central licence shrinks the field left to state food officers.
Process matters: the petition says a March 13, 2026 order raising the central licence threshold from Rs 20 crore to Rs 50 crore came without public consultation, violating the General Clauses Act.
GS2 · Rule of law / GS4 · Transparency
Changing licence thresholds without public consultation weakens the legitimacy of even a well-meant rule.
The Centre's case: enforcement has been inconsistent across and within states; a central mechanism ensures that 'at least bigger businesses always remain under the scanner'.
GS2 · Cooperative federalism
Uneven state enforcement is the Centre's argument; the answer is cooperative standards, not parallel inspectors.
keywords: A central body duplicating enforcement that a law gives to states
A parallel regulatory mechanism breeds turf wars and confuses businesses about whom to answer to.
Rules and orders made by an executive body under powers given by a statute
Delegated legislation must stay within the parent Act; orders creating central FSOs test that limit.
How regulatory powers are shared between national and state authorities
Food safety is a test of regulatory federalism: national standards, local enforcement.
Outcomes that rest on one officer's leadership rather than systems
A central official asked whether Maharashtra's good enforcement would survive one officer's transfer: institutions must outlast individuals.
examples: Licensing tiers under FSSAI
Registration up to Rs 1.5 crore turnover; state licence up to Rs 50 crore; central licence above Rs 50 crore or for inter-state, high-risk and export units
GS2 · Regulatory design
FSSAI's tiered licensing is an example of matching regulatory burden to business size.
'Proprietary foods' and Indian snacks
Inclusion first caught small samosa and mixture makers; FSSAI later added an exception
GS4
GS2 · Regulation and small business · GS4 · Proportionality
The samosa-maker exception shows why rules must be proportionate to the size of the business they hit.
pyqs: Recent changes in Centre-State relations; building trust.
National parties' centralisation vs regional parties' autonomy.
CBI jurisdiction in states; withholding consent.
CCI curbing abuse of dominance by MNCs.
State's role in containing marketisation of public healthcare.

trend.t: Centre–state questions have moved from constitutional devices (Article 356, 2023; Governors, 2022 and 2026) to everyday friction in shared domains: CBI consent (2021), building trust (2024) and fiscal federalism (2025). Regulatory bodies are asked one at a time (CCI 2023, tribunals 2025).
trend.watch: Centre–state relations have been asked every year from 2021 to 2026, increasingly through concrete disputes, so a regulator–state turf war like FSSAI is the kind of example UPSC now rewards.
focus: Concurrent-list domains: health, food, police cooperation
Delegated legislation and limits of regulators

potential: "Regulatory bodies are becoming a new site of Centre–state friction." Examine with reference to food safety regulation in India. (10 marks)
Discuss how cooperative federalism can be strengthened in regulatory domains shared by the Union and the States. (15 marks)

practice.q: "Regulatory bodies are becoming a new site of Centre–state friction." Examine with reference to food safety regulation in India.
parts: The case for a central role

answer.t: In 2026 Maharashtra moved the Bombay High Court alleging that FSSAI had built a 'parallel enforcement mechanism' that encroaches on state powers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

pts.t: Regulators expand roles through orders rather than amendments.
pts.ex: FSSAI's May 2023 order creating central FSOs, though the Act vests appointment in state Commissioners.

pts.t: Central licensing widened to new categories.
pts.ex: E-commerce platforms, five-star hotels, nutraceuticals and proprietary foods.

pts.t: Rules changed without consultation erode trust.
pts.ex: March 2026 threshold change from Rs 20 crore to Rs 50 crore without public consultation.

pts.t: States inspect but must report to the central authority, which runs proceedings.
pts.ex: Reports from state officers go to the central licensing authority.

answer.h: The case for a central role

pts.t: Enforcement varies across states and over time.
pts.ex: A central official's concern that one state's record depends on one officer.

pts.t: Inter-state and export businesses need one standard.
pts.ex: Central licence for businesses operating across state lines.

pts.t: If central enforcement is needed, Parliament should amend the Act.
Shared inspection protocols and data between FSSAI and state commissioners.
pts.ex: A food safety council on the GST Council model.

pts.t: Mandatory public and state consultation before rule changes.

answer.t: Food safety needs one standard and many hands: national rules enforced locally, with states treated as partners, not subordinates.

items.title: Karnataka widens ethanol probe to distribution network, CM slams Centre
items.syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; biofuels · GS2 › Issues in the federal structure · GS2 › Consumer protection (governance)
items.summary: Karnataka's probe into alleged excess ethanol blending in petrol has moved from pumps to blending and distribution agencies after lab tests found up to 31.2% ethanol against the E20 (20%) limit.
ideas: Policy goal vs quality control: ethanol blending cuts oil imports, but fuel above the E20 limit hurts vehicle performance and efficiency, and consumers bear the cost.
GS3 · Biofuels / energy security
Ethanol blending serves energy security only if blending norms are enforced; over-blending shifts the cost to motorists.
Evidence-led governance: samples from 67 locations were tested at NABL-accredited labs after oil companies allegedly did not share ethanol-content data.
GS2 · Transparency / consumer protection
Karnataka turned to independent NABL labs when data was not shared: testing as a tool of accountability.
Federal friction: fuel standards are central, but consumer complaints land on states; the CM said the Centre 'cannot shirk responsibility'.
GS2 · Centre–state relations
Fuel standards are set in Delhi but complaints reach state capitals, a gap that needs joint enforcement.
Consumer remedies proposed: action against violators, mandatory display of ethanol content at fuel stations, and compensation for vehicle damage linked to over-blending.
GS2 · Consumer rights / GS4 · Transparency
Displaying ethanol content at the pump is a simple transparency fix that restores consumer choice.
keywords: Petrol with 20% ethanol, the prescribed blend
E20 is India's blending benchmark; samples at 30% show why monitoring must keep pace with targets.
Certification of testing laboratories for reliable results
NABL-accredited testing gives a state's findings evidentiary weight against large oil companies.
Requiring sellers to display key product information
Mandatory disclosure of ethanol content would let motorists, not just regulators, hold sellers to account.
examples: Karnataka's 67-location fuel test
Up to 31.2% ethanol in an Indian Oil sample and 30.5% in an HPCL sample
GS4
GS2 · Evidence-based regulation · GS4 · Accountability
Karnataka's lab tests on petrol are an example of a state using evidence to hold big firms to account for consumers.
pyqs: Energy independence by 2047 through clean technology.
Recent changes in Centre-State relations; building trust.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewables targets (2022) to energy independence by 2047 (2025) and energy security challenges (2026); biofuels sit within this as an import-substitution tool.
trend.watch: Energy security was asked in 2025 and 2026, so the trade-offs of each tool, including ethanol blending's costs for consumers and food crops, are worth preparing.

potential: Ethanol blending serves India's energy security but raises concerns for consumers and food security. Discuss. (10 marks)

items.title: 'Implementation COP' must live up to its name
items.syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation; climate change · GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora (UNFCCC) · GS3 › Disaster management (adaptation, early warning)
items.summary: As COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, the editorial says it must narrow the gap between commitments and delivery: finance for clean energy in developing countries, adaptation and a funded Loss and Damage Fund.
evolution: Editorial and op-eds on looking beyond old climate fault lines ahead of COP31 (climate thread).
COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, billed as the 'Implementation COP'.
ideas: From pledges to delivery: COP30 at Belém secured outcomes on finance, adaptation and transition away from fossil fuels but fell short of the 1.5°C goal; overshooting 1.5°C now looks nearly inevitable.
GS3 · Climate change / GS2 · UNFCCC
The 'Implementation COP' label is an admission that the gap is now delivery, not ambition.
Unequal transition: emerging and developing economies outside China, with nearly two-thirds of the world's population, received just 18% of global clean-energy investment in 2025.
GS3 · Climate finance / equity
Two-thirds of humanity got 18% of clean-energy investment in 2025: the transition is unequal by design of finance.
Cost of capital: renewable projects in developing countries cost several times more to finance; high borrowing costs and public debt limit their transition.
GS3 · Climate finance
High cost of capital, not technology, is now the main barrier to clean energy in the Global South.
Just transition: countries like India cannot be expected to abandon fossil fuels at the pace of advanced economies without support; COP31 should remove barriers, not just urge higher targets.
GS2 · India's climate diplomacy
Just transition means barriers to deployment are removed before targets are raised.

Adaptation and loss and damage: early warning, resilient infrastructure and a Loss and Damage Fund with predictable, sufficient finance; the Nepal floods show least-emitting countries bear the steepest costs.
GS3 · Adaptation / disaster management
The Nepal floods show the injustice at climate's core: those who emitted least pay the most.
keywords: The distance between climate commitments and actual delivery
COP31's test is the implementation gap, not another round of pledges.
The interest and risk premium that makes projects costlier in poorer countries
A solar plant costs more in Africa than in Europe because of the cost of capital, not sunlight.
Moving to clean energy fairly, without leaving workers or poorer nations behind
India's case at COPs rests on a just transition backed by finance and technology.
Warming temporarily exceeding 1.5°C before any return
Near-certain overshoot of 1.5°C makes adaptation as urgent as mitigation.
data: Share of global clean-energy investment received in 2025 by emerging and developing economies outside China (nearly two-thirds of world population)
Developing economies outside China, home to two-thirds of humanity, got only 18% of clean-energy investment in 2025.
People in Africa still without electricity
Nearly 600 million Africans still lack electricity despite the continent's vast renewable potential.
examples: Nepal floods
Countries that contributed least to emissions face the steepest disaster costs
GS4
GS3 · Loss and damage · GS4 · Climate justice
The Nepal floods are an example of climate injustice: the least responsible pay the highest price.
Africa's energy paradox
Vast renewable potential, yet a fraction of investment and 600 million without power
GS3 · Energy access / GS2 · India–Africa
Africa's energy paradox shows that resources without finance do not light homes.
pyqs: India's climate policy in international fora.
Global warming as outcome of human greed in the name of development.

trend.t: Climate questions moved from treaty history (Kyoto, 2022) to COP outcomes and India's commitments (COP26 in 2021; NDC update in 2025) and India's diplomatic stance (2022). Adaptation enters through disaster resilience and Sendai targets (2024).
trend.watch: A COP-and-commitments question was asked in 2021 and 2025, so COP30–COP31 outcomes on finance, adaptation and loss and damage are likely material for the next one.
focus: Climate finance and the cost of capital
Adaptation and the Loss and Damage Fund
Climate justice as an ethics theme

potential: "The climate crisis is now a crisis of delivery, not of ambition." Examine in the context of COP31. (15 marks)
Why does clean energy remain costlier in developing countries? Suggest measures to close the climate finance gap. (10 marks)
Discuss the significance of the Loss and Damage Fund for countries like India and its neighbours. (10 marks)

practice.q: "The climate crisis is now a crisis of delivery, not of ambition." Examine in the context of COP31.

answer.t: COP31 opens in Antalya billed as the 'Implementation COP', a year after COP30 in Belém, with the world close to overshooting the 1.5°C limit set at Paris.

pts.k: Finance does not reach the South
pts.t: Clean-energy money is concentrated in rich economies and China.
pts.ex: Developing economies outside China got 18% of clean-energy investment in 2025.

pts.t: Renewable projects in developing countries cost several times more to finance.
pts.ex: High borrowing costs and public debt limit investment.

pts.t: Solar, EVs and storage are cheaper but adoption is uneven.
pts.ex: Africa's vast potential yet 600 million without electricity.

pts.t: Early warning and resilient infrastructure lag behind rising disasters.
pts.ex: Floods, heat waves and droughts more frequent since Belém.

pts.t: The fund lacks predictable and sufficient money.
pts.ex: Nepal floods: least emitters, steepest costs.

pts.t: Targets raised without removing barriers to deployment.
pts.ex: The editorial's call to address barriers 'rather than simply urging' higher targets.

pts.t: Existing commitments are inadequate.
Belém's transition outcome needs timelines.
pts.ex: Transition away from fossil fuels agreed at COP30.

pts.t: Extreme weather may intensify, raising stakes.
pts.ex: Threat of a super El Niño.

pts.t: Guarantees, blended finance and MDB reform for clean energy.
pts.ex: Risk-sharing for solar in Africa and South Asia.

pts.t: Differentiated pace with support for countries like India.
Early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure for vulnerable communities.
Predictable contributions to the Loss and Damage Fund.
pts.ex: Support for Himalayan countries like Nepal.

pts.t: Track finance delivered, not just pledged.
Share technology and finance models.

answer.t: COP31 will be judged not by new numbers but by whether a solar panel, a flood warning and a rebuilding fund actually reach those who need them.

items.title: Net Zero transition brings opportunity to build, not just import, technology
items.where: Editorial page, page 8 (Ramakrishna R Sonde, professor emeritus, BITS Pilani & Goa)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: indigenization of technology and developing new technology · GS3 › Industrial policy · GS3 › Climate change and energy transition
items.summary: India struggles to take research from the laboratory to industry; the author argues the Net Zero transition is a chance to build Indian technology by sharing development risk among government, academia and industry.
ideas: Atmanirbharta is more than assembly: manufacturing equipment while importing process know-how, materials, catalysts, designs and IP creates jobs but not technological independence.
GS3 · Indigenisation of technology
True atmanirbharta means owning the know-why and IP, not just assembling imported designs.
The 'valley of death': Indian academia works up to about TRL 3–4 while industry enters around TRL 7; the gap between lab validation and industrial demonstration is underfunded.
GS3 · R&D and innovation
Ideas die between TRL 4 and TRL 7, where neither academia nor industry is willing to pay.
Five recurring reasons: technology takes time and patient capital; industry wants proven technology; scale-up is complex; collaboration is weak; and nobody owns the journey.
GS3 · Innovation ecosystem
Technology development stalls because no one owns the journey from lab to plant.
Shared risk: government should carry more early-stage risk, industry's share should rise as uncertainty falls; deep-tech incubators and demonstration centres can bridge the gap.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Sharing development risk, with government taking the earliest bets, is how a new Indian technology gets proven.

Net Zero as an opening: green hydrogen, carbon capture, storage, sustainable fuels and circular manufacturing will reshape steel, cement, chemicals, fertilisers, transport and power; India can build new plants on new processes.
GS3 · Energy transition / industry
As India builds new steel, cement and fertiliser plants, it can build them on Indian technology rather than imported designs.
keywords: A nine-stage scale from basic idea to proven commercial deployment
Indian research stalls between TRL 4 and TRL 7, the stage of pilots and demonstration plants.
Knowing how to run a technology vs understanding why it works, which enables IP
Moving from know-how to know-why is what turns a manufacturer into a technology owner.
Long-horizon funding that accepts delays and failure
Deep-tech needs patient capital, which is why the state must share early risk.
Restrictions by other countries on access to advanced technology
Technology denial pushed India's atomic programme to build its own capabilities.
examples: India's atomic energy programme
Facing technology denial, India built its own capabilities through scientific leadership, freedom for scientists and acceptance of failure
GS4
GS3 · Indigenisation · GS4 · Leadership
The atomic programme shows that scientific leadership and tolerance of failure build indigenous technology.
Coal gasification for high-ash coal
Needs resources and commitment far beyond a successful R&D pilot plant
GS3 · Energy technology
Coal gasification suited to India's high-ash coal shows how scale-up, not invention, is the bottleneck.
pyqs: Energy independence by 2047 through clean technology.

trend.t: Science and technology questions have turned from general achievements to strategic indigenisation: the Semiconductor Mission, PLI and CCUS (all 2025) and energy independence through clean technology (2025).
trend.watch: Four 2025 questions touched indigenous technology for industry and energy, so the lab-to-industry gap and Atmanirbhar Bharat in clean technology are strong areas for the next paper.
focus: Lessons from atomic and space programmes

potential: "India must not settle for becoming merely a large market for technologies developed elsewhere." Discuss in the context of the Net Zero transition. (15 marks)

items.title: AI policy must take into account democratic bargain
items.where: Editorial page, page 8 (Ruchi Gupta, executive director, Future of India Foundation)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; employment · GS3 › Awareness in IT and emerging technology · GS2 › Government policies for development; vulnerable sections (youth) · Essay
items.summary: AI exposes fewer Indian jobs than in rich countries, yet India's development model is more vulnerable; the author proposes an AI and Work Observatory, apprenticeships, portable social protection and a parliamentary committee.
ideas: Three vulnerabilities: IT and entry-level cognitive work built India's middle class and consuming class; India has the world's largest youth population; and rich-country tools like UBI or public stakes in AI firms are not available.
GS3 · Employment / technology
AI threatens the very ladder, entry-level IT work, that built India's post-1991 middle class.
The broken pipeline: routine tasks AI now does are how inexperienced workers become experienced; cutting junior hiring weakens tomorrow's professionals.
GS3 · Skilling / labour market
If AI does junior work, the pipeline that produces senior professionals dries up.
Growth without jobs: offshored coding and support may move back in-house with AI; YouthPOWER analysis shows software exports growing while employment and real earnings weaken.
GS3 · Jobless growth
Software exports rising while jobs and real earnings fall is AI-era jobless growth.

Policy response: a national AI and Work Observatory; paid sectoral apprenticeships; human review of automated workplace decisions; portable social protection; a parliamentary committee hearing young people, workers, small firms and states.
GS2 · Policy design / participatory governance
Workers and young people must have a voice in setting the terms of AI adoption.
Demand for labour: 90% of young workers earn under Rs 20,000 a month; public investment in health, care, education, housing and urban services can create work where needs are unmet.
GS3 · Inclusive growth
Skilling improves access to work; only demand creates new work, through public investment in care and services.
keywords: The expectation that effort can improve one's circumstances, which sustains faith in democracy
AI policy must protect the democratic bargain: that effort leads to a better life.
Benefits that move with workers across jobs and employers
Portable social protection is the safety net for an AI-disrupted, job-hopping workforce.
Junior roles through which workers gain experience
AI's real threat is to the entry-level pipeline, not just to existing jobs.
Meaningful human review of automated decisions
Workers should have a human in the loop when algorithms decide on hiring or firing.
data: Share of young Indian workers earning less than Rs 20,000 a month
Ninety per cent of young Indian workers earn under Rs 20,000 a month, which limits demand and hiring.
examples: Work as dignity
Work gives competence, independence, social standing and a stake in the future
GS4
GS3 · Employment · GS4 · Dignity of labour
Work gives people competence, independence and standing, so an AI strategy must be judged by the work it creates.
pyqs: Linkages between education, skill and employment.
Fourth Industrial Revolution making e-governance integral to government.

trend.t: Employment questions moved from schemes (Make in India, Skill India, 2015) to the quality of growth: productivity-led job creation (2022), structural unemployment and the education–skill–job link (2023). AI entered as a technology question (agentic AI, 2026); the essay paper asked about AI and jobs in 2019.
trend.watch: AI was asked in 2026 as technology and jobs questions recur every year, so the overlap, AI's effect on entry-level work and on youth, is a likely next question.
focus: AI and the entry-level job ladder
Social protection for gig and AI-era workers
Demand-side job creation in care and services

potential: "India must judge its AI strategy by whether it expands access to productive work and upward mobility." Discuss. (15 marks)
How does artificial intelligence threaten the entry-level job pipeline in India? Suggest policy measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India must judge its AI strategy by whether it expands access to productive work and upward mobility." Discuss.
parts: Why AI is a particular risk for India

answer.t: Fewer Indian jobs are directly exposed to AI than in advanced economies, yet India's development model, built on IT services and a young workforce, is more vulnerable.

answer.h: Why AI is a particular risk for India

pts.t: IT and entry-level cognitive work created India's consuming class after liberalisation.
pts.ex: Disruption would spread to sectors that depend on their spending.

pts.t: The world's largest youth population needs productive jobs, unlike ageing economies.
pts.ex: Graduate unemployment is higher than for young people as a whole.

pts.t: Routine tasks are how juniors learn; firms may hire fewer of them.

items.title: AI and cybersecurity: Can it find flaws without creating new risks?
items.syllabus: GS3 › Basics of cyber security · GS3 › Awareness in IT and emerging technology · GS4 › Applied ethics (dual-use technology)
items.summary: October 2026, dubbed 'Black October', saw major cyber incidents found with AI's help, including the PHP2Shell flaws; AI makes finding vulnerabilities easier, but leaks, patching races and costs raise new risks.
evolution: CERT-In sets a six-hour reporting deadline for AI security incidents (cyber thread).
ideas: AI as a double-edged sword: AI-assisted techniques uncovered exploits first theorised in 2004, but the same tools help attackers.
GS3 · Cyber security / emerging tech
AI finds old flaws faster, for defenders and attackers alike, making cyber security a race.
Scale of exposure: around 70% of websites reportedly run some version of PHP, so PHP2Shell could affect innumerable sites; exploit details leaked before a patch.
GS3 · Critical information infrastructure
One flaw in a language used by 70% of websites shows how concentrated digital risk has become.
Fragile commons: much patching of open-source software is done by volunteers, while attackers can target hundreds of millions of systems.
GS3 · Cyber security
The internet rests on volunteer-maintained open-source code, a public good that needs public support.
Limits of proof: formal verification can prove systems meet requirements, but proofs are only as good as their assumptions; a proof of correctness is not freedom from all flaws.
GS3 · Technology
Even mathematically verified code is only as safe as the assumptions behind it.
Conflict of interest and costs: AI firms that expose vulnerabilities could also sell protection; data centres raise environmental concerns.
GS4 · Applied ethics
When the firm that finds a flaw also sells the fix, cyber security becomes an ethics question.
keywords: A software flaw unknown to the maker, exploitable before a patch
AI shortens the time to find vulnerabilities, so patching speed becomes national security.
Proving mathematically that a system meets its specification
Formal verification raises assurance but cannot remove the need for human judgement on assumptions.
Technology usable for both protection and harm
AI in cyber security is a classic dual-use technology.
examples: 'Black October' 2026
eMudhra weak keys, PHP2Shell, the LiteLLM hack and a GitLab flaw within days
GS3 · Cyber threats
'Black October' 2026 shows how AI has speeded up the discovery of serious cyber flaws.
Volunteer patching of PHP
Much of the fix was done by volunteers like Czech programmer Ondřej Surý
GS4
GS3 · Open source · GS4 · Public spirit
Volunteers patching global code show public-spirited service sustaining a digital commons.

trend.t: Cyber security questions moved from policy (2013 policy, 2015) to attack types (2020), cross-border attacks (2021) and national strategy (2022), then to data protection (2024) and IT Rules on fake news (2026). AI itself was asked in 2026.
trend.watch: Cyber security is asked almost every year and AI entered in 2026, so AI-enabled cyber threats and defences are a natural next question.
focus: AI in cyber offence and defence

potential: "Artificial intelligence is both the strongest shield and the sharpest sword in cyber security." Discuss. (10 marks)

items.title: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data centre impacts
items.syllabus: GS3 › Conservation; biodiversity · GS3 › Science and technology in everyday life · GS3 › Climate change · GS4 › Environmental ethics
items.summary: Conservation groups use AI to track forest fires and count wildlife but worry about the electricity and water used by data centres; the trade-offs are expected to feature at COP31.
ideas: AI for conservation: real-time wildfire alerts to community patrols in Cambodia; AI analysis of 200,000 aerial images in hours in Kenya instead of nine people over nine months.
GS3 · Biodiversity / technology
AI turns months of wildlife counting into hours, making conservation faster and cheaper.
Better data, better protection: AI surveys found human counts had missed about a third of elephants and roughly half of zebras and giraffes; accurate data can secure conservation finance.
GS3 · Conservation finance
Better wildlife data makes 'nature measurable and therefore investable'.

The footprint: the IEA estimates data centres will use about 945 TWh of electricity a year by 2030, equal to over 300 million tonnes of CO2; water use could rise from 560 billion litres (2023) to 1.2 trillion litres by 2030.
GS3 · Climate / water
AI's promise for the planet comes with a planetary bill in electricity and water.
Disclosure: the UN Secretary-General wants AI companies to disclose their systems' environmental impact.
GS2 · Global governance / GS4 · Transparency
Mandatory disclosure of AI's energy and water use is the first step to sustainable AI.
keywords: Developing and deploying AI within environmental limits
Sustainable AI asks not only what AI can do for nature, but what it costs nature.
Measuring ecosystems well enough to attract finance
AI-based counts can make nature investable by proving conservation outcomes.
data: Projected annual electricity use of global data centres, equal to over 300 million tonnes of CO2
The IEA projects data centres will use about 945 TWh of electricity a year by 2030.
Data-centre water use may double to 1.2 trillion litres by 2030, the IEA estimates.

Machine learning to count wildlife and study elephant communication
GS3 · Technology for biodiversity
Kenya's AI-led wildlife census shows technology strengthening conservation at scale.
Gombe chimpanzee notes
AI used to digitise decades of Jane Goodall's field notes
GS3 · Science and conservation
Digitising Gombe's field notes shows AI preserving and reusing scientific knowledge.

Energy and water footprint of data centres
