items.title: The mud kitchen in Kangra breathes with the seasons
items.syllabus: GS1 › Indian heritage (vernacular architecture) · GS3 › Disaster management (landslides, earthquakes) · GS3 › Environment · GS2 › Government policies (PMAY, building codes) · Essay
items.summary: Concrete homes in Himachal trap heat and damp and load fragile slopes, while traditional mud, stone and timber houses suit the climate and quakes; codes, PMAY rules and banks still favour cement.
ideas: Climate-wise tradition: thick mud, local stone and slate kitchens stay cool in summer and warm in winter; concrete rooms trap heat and become 'damp iceboxes'.
GS1 · Vernacular architecture / GS3 · Climate adaptation
Kangra's mud kitchen is passive climate control that needs no AC or heater.

Disaster-resilient heritage: kath-kuni (deodar timber and dry stone), dhajji-dewari (timber and mud) and Spiti's rammed earth evolved for earthquakes; stone foundations drain water while concrete blocks it.
GS3 · Disaster management / GS1 · Heritage
Kath-kuni and dhajji-dewari are earthquake engineering inherited from Himalayan ancestors.

Unplanned concrete boom: CEC figures show hotels grew 90% and homestays 670% (2016–2025); GSI linked 2023 landslides in Kullu, Mandi and Shimla to blocked drainage, multi-storey weight and 90-degree hill cuts.
GS3 · Landslides / carrying capacity
The 2023 Himachal landslides show concrete without carrying-capacity studies turning rain into disaster.

Systems biased against tradition: building codes, PWD schedules, bylaws, PMAY rules and bank loans favour cement; forest laws trap bartandari timber rights; the 'pucca vs kutcha' mindset stigmatises mud.
GS2 · Policy design / GS1 · Social attitudes
Labelling mud homes 'kutcha' has pushed an ecological wisdom out of codes, loans and minds.
Fixes: recognise engineered mud, kath-kuni and dhajji-dewari as pucca, insurable and loan-eligible; ITIs to teach earth building and pay thawis (master masons) to train.
GS2 · Housing policy / GS3 · Resilient infrastructure
Making traditional homes loan-eligible under PMAY would align housing policy with disaster resilience.
keywords: The development load an area can bear without degradation
Himachal's slopes were built on without carrying-capacity studies, and the 2023 landslides followed.
Local building traditions shaped by climate and materials
Vernacular architecture is climate adaptation that predates the climate crisis.
Himachali technique of interlocking deodar timber and dry stone
Kath-kuni walls flex in earthquakes, while concrete cracks.
The Supreme Court's 2025 principle while rejecting a hotel on Shimla's forested slopes
The SC's 'ecology must come before revenue' sets the test for hill development.
data: Growth in registered hotels and homestays in Himachal, 2016–2025
Central Empowered Committee (cited by the author)
Himachal's homestays grew 670% in a decade, much of it concrete on unstable slopes.
examples: Thawis of Himachal
Traditional master masons and woodcarvers who are disappearing
GS4
GS1 · Heritage · GS4 · Dignity of labour
Young helpers calling mudwork 'dirty' shows how lost dignity of labour erodes traditional skills.
GSI on 2023 Himachal landslides
Linked to blocked drainage, heavy buildings and 90-degree hill cuts
GS3 · Landslides / Himalayan disasters
The GSI's 2023 findings show landslides in Himachal are partly man-made.
pyqs: Fast infrastructure vs disaster-risk reduction in fragile areas.

trend.t: Disaster questions shifted from describing hazards (landslides 2021, cloudbursts 2022, 2024) to governance: resilience and Sendai targets (2024), and in 2026 both fast infrastructure versus risk reduction in fragile areas and community participation.
trend.watch: Two 2026 questions asked about development in fragile areas and community roles, so Himalayan construction, building codes and traditional knowledge are high-value material.

potential: "Traditional knowledge can be a strong ally in disaster risk reduction in the Himalayas." Discuss with examples. (15 marks)
How do building norms and housing schemes shape disaster vulnerability in hill states? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Traditional knowledge can be a strong ally in disaster risk reduction in the Himalayas." Discuss with examples.

answer.t: After the 2023 monsoon disasters, the Geological Survey of India linked landslides in Kullu, Mandi and Shimla to blocked drainage, heavy multi-storey buildings and 90-degree hill cuts, not just to rain.

pts.t: Interlocking timber and dry stone flex instead of cracking.
pts.ex: Kath-kuni in Kullu and Shimla; dhajji-dewari in Kangra and Chamba.

pts.t: Stone foundations let rainwater drain; concrete blocks it and loads slopes.
pts.ex: GSI findings on blocked drainage in 2023.

pts.t: Mud walls keep homes cool in summer and warm in winter, reducing energy use.
Lighter structures suit fragile slopes.
Settlements traditionally avoided unstable slopes and streams.
Traditional masons maintain safe practices.
Building codes, PWD price lists and bylaws obstruct mud-and-stone plans.
pts.ex: National Building Code and fire bylaws.

pts.t: PMAY favours brick and cement; banks deny loans and insurance for mud homes.
Forest laws trapped villagers' bartandari timber rights in red tape.
pts.ex: 1980 Forest Conservation Act and 1996 felling limits.

pts.t: Mudwork seen as 'dirty' and concrete as modern.
Few artisans and costly natural-building architects.
Tourism boom drives quick concrete construction.
Recognise engineered mud, kath-kuni and dhajji-dewari as pucca and insurable.
Make traditional designs eligible under PMAY and for bank loans.
ITIs to teach earth building; pay master masons to train.
Mandatory studies before multi-storey construction on slopes.
Apply the Supreme Court's principle to hill projects.
Use local knowledge in village disaster plans.

answer.t: When monsoon clouds burst or fault lines shift, what bends survives: Himalayan resilience may lie less in a cement bag than in the wisdom of a mud kitchen.

items.title: Next on nation's to-do list: More productive jobs
items.where: Ideas page, page 9 (Tejasvi Surya, BJP MP, and Kishen Shastry, University of Cambridge); HSBC report on Economy page, page 13
items.syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; employment; mobilisation of resources · GS2 › Welfare schemes and delivery (DBT) · GS2 › Fiscal federalism · Essay
items.summary: The authors credit India's sharp fall in extreme poverty to growth, state capacity and DBT, and say the next task is productive jobs through state-level reforms, which is at risk from states' subsidy burden.
evolution: World Bank: extreme poverty falls to 2.6% in 2023 (poverty thread).
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
Two Ideas-page pieces on the same World Bank brief; HSBC flags falling real rural wages.
ideas: Additive and subtractive reform: unlike Reagan or Thatcher, India had to build basic state capacity (toilets, bank accounts, IDs, roads, ports) while reforming institutions (GST, IBC), facing 19th- and 21st-century problems at once.
GS2 · Governance / GS3 · Reforms
India's reform has been additive and subtractive: building the state's reach while removing barriers.

Poverty decline, as per the World Bank: extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011) to 2.6% (2023), and close to 50 crore people crossed the lower-middle-income line, credited to consumption growth, rising employment (especially women) and social transfers.
GS3 · Poverty / inclusive growth
Extreme poverty fell from 27.1% to 2.6% between 2011 and 2023, according to the World Bank.
Delivery architecture: DBT was revived and scaled on identity, bank accounts and payment rails across hundreds of schemes, cutting leakages; digital public infrastructure enabled social protection.
GS2 · E-governance / welfare delivery
DBT on Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and payment rails turned leaky subsidies into direct transfers.

The next frontier lies with states: reforms in power, land, urban planning and agricultural markets are in state hands, but states spend over Rs 3 lakh crore on subsidies, and with salaries, pensions and interest, over 90% of revenue receipts.
GS2 · Fiscal federalism / GS3 · Fiscal policy
Productive jobs need state reforms, but subsidies and committed spending leave states little fiscal space.
Counterpoint: HSBC says falling real rural wages 'cannot be ignored', with investment intentions rising only in value terms; job quality, not just poverty counts, is the real test.
GS3 · Employment and wages
Poverty is down, but falling real rural wages show that productive jobs remain the unfinished task.
keywords: The ability of the state to deliver services and enforce policy
The last decade showed India can build state capacity at scale; the next must sustain reform across states.
Room in a budget for new spending after committed expenditure
Subsidies eat the fiscal space states need for reforms that create jobs.
Salaries, pensions and interest that a government must pay
When committed expenditure and subsidies exceed 90% of revenue, capital spending suffers.
A state focused on building infrastructure at speed (from the book Breakneck)
India combines the ambition of an engineering state with the checks of a multiparty democracy.
data: Extreme poverty in India, 2011 to 2023 ($3/day, 2021 PPP)
World Bank India Poverty and Equity Brief, October 2026
The World Bank says India's extreme poverty fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023.
People who moved above the lower-middle-income poverty line, 2011–2023
Close to 50 crore Indians moved above the lower-middle-income poverty line in 12 years.
examples: Karnataka's subsidy bill
Over Rs 1 lakh crore budgeted for subsidies, close to a third of revenue receipts (authors' figure)
GS3 · State finances
Karnataka's subsidy bill, about a third of its revenue, shows how welfare can crowd out investment.
DBT for cooking gas
Started reluctantly, abandoned before 2014, then revived and scaled
GS4
GS2 · Welfare delivery · GS4 · Good governance
The revival of DBT shows good governance: plugging leakages so benefits reach the intended citizen.
pyqs: Inequality in resource ownership and the 'paradox of poverty'.
Managing inflation and unemployment to serve the poor, beyond welfare schemes.

trend.t: Poverty questions moved from measurement (MPI, 2020) to the limits of welfare (beyond schemes, 2022; DBT limitations, 2022) and inequality (paradox of poverty, 2025); state finances entered with the Fiscal Health Index (2025).
trend.watch: The 2022 and 2025 questions both asked what lies beyond welfare transfers, so productive jobs and state fiscal health are likely angles.

potential: "India has shown it can reduce poverty through state capacity; it must now show it can create productive jobs." Discuss. (15 marks)

items.title: With decline in poverty, shift focus — from free food to nutritional security
items.where: Ideas page, page 9 (Ashok Gulati, Ritika Juneja and Sulakshana Rao, ICRIER)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Food security; public distribution system; buffer stocks · GS3 › Agriculture: soil health, biofortification · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty and hunger; malnutrition
items.summary: Using the World Bank brief, the authors argue that with extreme poverty at 2.6%, free grain to 81 crore people under PM-GKY should be rationalised and reoriented to nutrition: food coupons, biofortified staples and healthier soils.
ideas: Inflection point 2004: poverty ($4.20/day) fell only 0.2% a year in 1983–2004 but about 7.2% a year after; drivers were growth, falling population growth and agriculture.
GS3 · Growth and poverty
India's poverty decline accelerated after 2004 as growth rose and population growth slowed.
Agriculture reduces poverty most: per capita agricultural GVA growth more than doubled; the World Development Report 2008 found farm growth at least 2.5 times more potent in reducing poverty.
GS3 · Agriculture and poverty
Growth from agriculture cuts poverty at least 2.5 times faster than growth from other sectors.
A paradox: farm employment rose to 46.5% in 2020-21 before settling at 43%; real farm wages are broadly flat and new jobs are in low-productivity work, limiting rural demand.
GS3 · Employment / rural economy
When labour cannot leave farming, wages stagnate and rural demand for manufactured goods stays weak.

Rationalise PM-GKY: free grain to about 81 crore people (Rs 2.27 lakh crore in 2026-27) is hard to justify with extreme poverty at 2.6%; the authors suggest Vajpayee's formula, free for Antyodaya and at least half the procurement price for others.
GS3 · Food subsidies / PDS
Free grain for more than half the population needs rationalisation now that extreme poverty is 2.6%.

From calories to nutrition: child malnutrition remains high; wheat and rice lack iron and zinc due to impoverished soils (SOC about 0.3% vs a desirable 1.5–2.0%); give food coupons for millets, pulses, milk and eggs and biofortify staples.
GS3 · Nutrition security / soil health
Nutrition security begins in the soil: depleted organic carbon gives us staples poor in iron and zinc.
keywords: Access to a diet with adequate nutrients, not just calories
India has achieved food security; nutrition security is the next goal.
Carbon in soil that sustains fertility and nutrient uptake
India's SOC of about 0.3% against a desirable 1.5–2% explains nutrient-poor grain.
Breeding crops richer in micronutrients like iron and zinc
Biofortified wheat and rice can fight hidden hunger through the PDS.
Free wheat and rice fill stomachs but not the gap of hidden hunger.
data: PM-GKY gives free grain to about 81 crore people at Rs 2.27 lakh crore in 2026-27.
India's soil organic carbon against the desirable level
World Food Laureate Rattan Lal (cited by the authors)
India's soil organic carbon is around 0.3%, against a desirable 1.5–2%, says Rattan Lal.
How much more potent agricultural growth is in reducing poverty than other growth
The WDR 2008 found farm growth at least 2.5 times more effective at cutting poverty.
examples: China's farm reforms, 1978–84
Raised rural incomes, which created demand for manufactured goods through town and village enterprises
GS3 · Agriculture-led industrialisation
China's 1978–84 farm reforms show rural incomes fuelling a manufacturing revolution.
'Teach a man to fish'
Better to build capability than hand out free food every day
GS4
GS3 · Welfare design · GS4 · Dignity and self-reliance
Welfare should empower people to earn, not create permanent dependence.
pyqs: Malnutrition as challenge of social equity, human development, welfare governance.
Breaking the vicious cycle of poverty and malnutrition for human capital.
Millets for health and nutritional security.

trend.t: Food questions moved from distribution (PDS reforms, 2019 and 2022; NFSA, 2021) to nutrition (millets, 2024; poverty–malnutrition cycle, 2024) and in 2026 malnutrition as a challenge of equity and welfare governance.
trend.watch: Malnutrition was asked in 2024 and 2026, and PDS in 2019 and 2022, so the shift 'from food security to nutrition security' is a must-study theme.
focus: Nutrition: millets, pulses, milk and eggs

potential: "India has moved from food scarcity to food security; it must now move to nutrition security." Discuss. (15 marks)
Examine the case for rationalising free food grain under PM-GKY. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India has moved from food scarcity to food security; it must now move to nutrition security." Discuss.

answer.t: The World Bank's October 2026 brief shows India's extreme poverty fell to 2.6% in 2023, yet child malnutrition remains high, so the challenge has moved from calories to nutrients.

pts.t: The National Food Security Act, 2013 made food a right.
Free grain to about 81 crore people.
pts.ex: PM-GKY extended for five years from 2024.

pts.t: Allocations were enhanced to 10 kg per person per month during Covid.
Transfers contributed to falling poverty.
PDS gives wheat and rice, not diverse diets.
pts.ex: Millets, pulses, milk and eggs largely outside PDS.

pts.t: Wheat and rice are deficient in iron and zinc.
Low soil organic carbon reduces nutrient content.
Under-five malnutrition remains very high.
Free grain for over half the population costs heavily.
Flat real farm wages limit diet diversity.
pts.ex: World Bank brief on real earnings.

pts.t: Free for the poorest, part-price for others.
Let families buy healthier foods from designated stores.
Iron- and zinc-rich wheat and rice in the PDS.
Raise soil organic carbon through organic matter and crop diversity.
Shift incentives from rice and wheat to pulses and millets.
Link PDS with Poshan, ICDS and school meals.

answer.t: Viksit Bharat cannot be built on full stomachs and empty plates of nutrients; nutrition security must start in the soil and end on the child's plate.

items.title: 2-child norm for panchayat polls: Why SC says it's time for a rethink
items.syllabus: GS2 › Devolution of powers to local levels; local self-government · GS2 › Fundamental rights; judiciary · GS1 › Population; role of women · GS4 › Inclusive governance
items.summary: Explainer on the Supreme Court's referral of Javed v. State of Haryana (2003) to a larger Bench: with TFR at 1.9, the fear of overpopulation behind two-child rules for panchayat polls 'has crumbled'.
evolution: SC refers its 2003 ruling to a larger Bench (first card on the two-child norm).
Explained: the legal framework, Javed (2003) and what the court said now.
ideas: The law: Maharashtra's 1995 amendment disqualifies anyone with more than two children from Gram Panchayat office; Haryana, Rajasthan, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh have similar rules.
GS2 · Local self-government
Several states bar people with more than two children from panchayat office, a population-control tool from the 1990s.
Javed (2003): a three-judge Bench upheld the rule; there is no Article 21 right to procreate without consequence for holding office, and contesting an election is a statutory, not fundamental, right.
GS2 · Fundamental rights / judiciary
Javed held that contesting elections is a statutory right that legislatures may condition.
Changed facts: TFR fell from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9, below replacement (2.1); ignoring this would be 'dangerously complacent'; policies must be 'in tune with the present realities'.
GS1 · Population / GS2 · Evolving jurisprudence
With TFR at 1.9, a law built on fear of overpopulation has lost its basis.
Unequal application: the Bench asked why such conditions apply only to panchayat representatives and not to MPs or MLAs.
GS2 · Equality / grassroots democracy
Barring only panchayat candidates places a burden on grassroots democracy that Parliament does not bear.
Gendered harm: unlike Javed, which saw equal effects on men and women, the Bench said in a patriarchal society the norm 'tended to weaken the position of women rather than empowering them'.
GS1 · Women / GS4 · Inclusive governance
In a patriarchal society, a two-child bar shuts women out of panchayats rather than empowering them.
keywords: TFR of about 2.1, at which a population replaces itself
India's TFR of 1.9 is below replacement level, turning the population debate on its head.
A right created by law vs one guaranteed by the Constitution
Because contesting is a statutory right, legislatures can attach conditions, but they must still be reasonable.
data: India's total fertility rate when Javed was decided and now (replacement level: 2.1)
India's fertility rate has fallen from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1.
examples: Maharashtra woman sarpanch's plea
Led to the referral of Javed to a larger Bench
GS4
GS2 · Local democracy · GS4 · Inclusion of women
A woman sarpanch challenging the two-child bar shows why inclusive governance must open, not narrow, the gates of local office.
pyqs: Women's reservation in local government and patriarchal politics.
'Demographic winter' — is the world heading there?
Challenges of demographic transition in India.

trend.t: Demography questions turned from population control (women's empowerment and population, 2019) to ageing and decline ('demographic winter', 2024; demographic transition, 2026). Local government questions keep returning to women's representation (2019, 2026).
trend.watch: Demographic transition was asked in 2024 and 2026, so laws built for a high-fertility India, like the two-child norm, are strong examples.

potential: "Laws built for a high-fertility India may now hurt grassroots democracy." Examine with reference to two-child norms for panchayat elections. (10 marks)

items.title: Meet the Siddis: Tribal Gujaratis from Kathiawad, natural athletes of African stock
items.syllabus: GS1 › Salient features of Indian society; diversity · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections (Scheduled Tribes, PVTGs) · GS4 › Inclusive governance; equity; compassion towards the weaker sections
items.summary: Khushbu Darjada, 15, became the first Siddi athlete to win a Youth Olympics medal (judo silver); the Siddis of Gujarat, of African descent, are a PVTG of about 12,959 people.
ideas: Diversity of Indian society: the Siddis, of East African descent, speak Gujarati with a Kathiawadi accent and share local food and dress; their faith blends Sufi Islam with local Hindu elements.
GS1 · Diversity / syncretism
The Siddis of Kathiawad show India's diversity: African roots, Gujarati culture and a Sufi-Hindu blend.
History of arrival: views differ, Portuguese colonists as slaves, overland via invaders, or as bodyguards invited by the nawabs of Junagadh; there is no definitive record.
GS1 · History / migration
The Siddis' many origin stories show how slavery, trade and princely courts shaped Indian society.

Classification and inclusion: declared ST in 1956 and a 'primitive tribal group' in 1982; Siddis in Saurashtra are STs but those outside are SEBC, so the same community gets different protection by place.
GS2 · Scheduled Tribes / PVTGs
Siddis are STs in Saurashtra but SEBC elsewhere in Gujarat: classification by geography can fragment protection.
Sport as a ladder: young Siddis are selected for sports camps, but many drop out, unable to cope with the discipline; the Darjada sisters show what sustained support can achieve.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections / GS4 · Inclusive governance
Sports camps open a door for Siddi youth; mentoring and support must keep it open.
Education as change: Afsana Makwa became the first Siddi woman to clear the Gujarat PSC exam; more youths are completing higher education, though such families are still few.
GS1 · Social change / GS4 · Equity
The first Siddi woman to clear the state PSC shows education turning a marginalised community into a participating one.
keywords: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, marked by small, stagnant population and low development
The Siddis are among 75 PVTGs who need targeted, culturally sensitive development.
Equity gives extra support to those who start behind; equality treats all alike
Sports quotas and coaching for Siddi youth are equity, not favour.
Blending of different religious and cultural traditions
Siddi rituals that mix Sufi Islam and Hindu practice are an example of Indian syncretism.
examples: Khushbu Darjada, Youth Olympics 2026
First Siddi athlete, and only the second Indian, to win a Youth Olympics judo medal
GS4
GS2 · Vulnerable sections · GS4 · Inclusive governance
Khushbu Darjada's medal shows that inclusive governance, giving opportunity to the margins, enriches the nation.
Afsana Makwa
First woman from the Siddi community to clear the Gujarat Public Service Commission exam
GS4
GS1 · Women and social change · GS4 · Equity
Afsana Makwa's success shows education as the surest ladder for marginalised women.
pyqs: Does tribal development policy reflect equity-based governance?
When diverse tribes can be treated as one category.
Legal initiatives against discrimination of STs.

trend.t: Tribal questions moved from constitutional basis (2016) and discrimination (2017) to whether diverse tribes can be one category (2022), displacement (2025) and, in 2026, whether tribal policy reflects equity-based governance.
trend.watch: The 2026 question asked about equity in tribal policy, so examples of inclusion, and of gaps like differing ST status by region, are valuable.
focus: Sport and education as ladders of mobility

potential: "Inclusive governance is measured by the opportunities it creates at the margins." Discuss with reference to Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. (10 marks)

items.title: Gender struggles must forge solidarities, not exclusion
items.where: Ideas page, page 9 (Swarupa Deb, human rights lawyer and sociologist)
items.syllabus: GS2 › Fundamental rights; mechanisms for protection of vulnerable sections (transgender persons) · GS1 › Social empowerment; women · GS4 › Social justice; equity; inclusive governance
items.summary: A women's group has asked the Supreme Court to stop recognising trans women as 'females' in official documents; the author argues debate must treat transgender persons as equal rights-bearers, not as a threat to women.
ideas: The petition: a women's group argues that recognising trans women as females could affect sex-based reservation, sporting categories, women-only spaces and safeguards for women.
GS2 · Rights in conflict
The petition sets women's sex-based protections against trans women's legal recognition.
Feminism's own critique: feminist movements contested the idea that biology or reproductive capacity determines women's social position, which in turn helped the transgender movement.
GS1 · Women's movements
Feminism argued anatomy is not destiny, a principle that also underpins transgender recognition.

History of solidarity: trans and cis feminists worked together on bodily autonomy in the 1970s; in November 2019 Indian women's groups opposed making recognition depend on certification by authorities and medical documents.
GS1 · Social movements / GS2 · Self-identification
In 2019, Indian women's groups stood with trans persons for self-determined gender identity.
Equality is indivisible: the constitutional guarantee of equality cannot be upheld if one marginalised group's protection is secured at the expense of another.
GS2 · Equality (Art 14) / GS4 · Social justice
Rights secured by excluding another marginalised group weaken equality for all.

Debate, but on equal terms: the issues of gender identity, sex-based classification and legal protections need reasoned debate premised on recognising transgender persons as equal rights-bearing subjects.
GS2 · Rights / GS4 · Inclusive governance
Hard questions on gender and law deserve debate, but only one that begins from equal dignity.
keywords: The right to determine one's own gender identity without medical certification
Self-identification of gender was upheld as part of dignity and autonomy.
Joint action by groups facing overlapping discrimination
Intersectional solidarity between women's and trans rights movements strengthens both.
The right to make decisions about one's own body
Bodily autonomy links reproductive rights and gender identity under Article 21.
examples: Women's groups' statement, November 2019
Opposed provisions making transgender recognition depend on state and medical certification
GS4
GS1 · Social movements · GS4 · Solidarity and empathy
The 2019 statement by women's groups shows empathy across struggles, a value inclusive governance needs.
pyqs: Effect of 2026 amendment to Transgender Persons Act 2019 on self-identity and privacy (Art 21).
Constitutional perspectives on gender justice, provisions and case laws.
Are welfare schemes for vulnerable sections discriminatory by nature?
Gender equality, gender equity and women's empowerment.

trend.t: Gender questions broadened from women's empowerment (2019, 2024) to constitutional gender justice (2023) and, in 2026, the rights of transgender persons under the amended Transgender Persons Act.
trend.watch: Transgender rights were asked directly in 2026, and rights-in-conflict framing is UPSC's favoured pattern, so the recognition debate is high-yield.
focus: Transgender Persons Act and its 2026 amendment

potential: "The constitutional guarantee of equality cannot be upheld by securing one marginalised group's rights at the expense of another." Discuss in the context of transgender rights. (15 marks)

items.title: Raipur man who went to Russia for job lands in jail, now family seeks CM, police's help
items.syllabus: GS2 › Indian diaspora; welfare of Indians abroad · GS2 › Effect of policies and politics of other countries on India's interests · GS4 › Compassion towards the weaker sections; citizen-centric governance
items.summary: A Raipur store manager who left for Russia on a tourist visa after a job offer on Telegram says he is jailed on false charges and pressured to join the Russian army; his family has written to the CM, police and the PM's grievance portal.
ideas: A pattern, not a one-off: a 21-year-old from Bilaspur also went to Russia on a tourist visa after a Telegram job offer; neither family knew the nature of the work.
GS2 · Protection of Indians abroad
Repeated Telegram job offers that end in Russian detention point to an organised recruitment racket.
War's reach into Indian homes: men lured by jobs are allegedly pressured to sign consent to join the Russian military in the war against Ukraine.
GS2 · India–Russia relations / effect of conflicts on India
Indians forced into Russia's war show how distant conflicts reach poor families in India.
Slow and layered response: the complaint moves from the police commissionerate to the state home department to the MEA; the embassy said it was 'trying to ascertain the details'.
GS2 · Consular services / federal coordination
A family's plea passes through police, state and MEA, while a detained man waits.
Prevention gaps: tourist visas used for jobs, unregulated recruiters on social media and lack of pre-departure awareness among job seekers.
GS2 · Migration governance
Unregulated online recruitment needs the same scrutiny as licensed overseas recruiters.
keywords: Moving abroad out of economic pressure, often through risky channels
Distress migration through fake job offers turns aspiration into captivity.
A state's duty to assist its citizens in trouble abroad
Swift consular protection is the most visible duty a state owes its citizens abroad.
Administration designed around the citizen's needs, not files
A detained citizen's family should not have to knock on every door: that is the test of citizen-centric governance.
examples: Telegram job offers to Russia
Two Chhattisgarh men travelled on tourist visas and ended up detained or pressured to join the military
GS4
GS2 · Diaspora protection · GS4 · Compassion towards the weaker sections
The Chhattisgarh cases show why compassion towards the weaker sections must include citizens trapped abroad.
pyqs: Benefits of Indian diaspora in the West.
Diaspora as bridge turning heritage into geopolitical influence.

trend.t: Diaspora questions have looked at the benefits and influence of Indians abroad (2017, 2020, 2023, 2026); protection of vulnerable migrants has not been asked directly, but labour migration trends were (2015).
trend.watch: The diaspora was asked in 2023 and 2026, but only as an asset; the protection side, recruitment rackets and conflict zones, is a gap worth covering.
focus: Regulation of overseas recruiters and online offers

potential: "India's diaspora policy must protect the vulnerable migrant as much as it celebrates the successful one." Discuss. (10 marks)

items.title: Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged after Houthi attack
items.where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Reuters, Riyadh)
items.syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (West Asia) · GS3 › Energy security
items.summary: Debris from an attempted Houthi attack damaged an Aramco building in Riyadh; the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities since fighting resumed in July as part of the wider war that followed US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
evolution: Energy security after the Hormuz shock: Iran exempts Indian ships (energy thread).
ideas: Widening war: the Houthi front reopened in July as part of the Middle East war reignited by US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered truce.
GS2 · West Asia
The collapse of the 2022 Yemen truce shows how one war in West Asia spreads to many fronts.
Energy infrastructure as target: Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities are being hit; Aramco's headquarters suffered extensive damage in October and a Riyadh airport attack killed 13.
GS3 · Energy security
Attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure put India's crude supply and prices at risk.
For India: crude oil prices are seen as the biggest factor for Indian markets; a recent rally coincided with crude falling to about $90 a barrel (p. 2).
GS3 · Energy security / economy
Every strike on Gulf oil assets travels to India through the price of crude.
keywords: Oil fields, terminals and pipelines vital to supply
Protecting critical energy infrastructure abroad is beyond India's control, so diversification is the answer.
Spreading crude imports across sources and routes
Diversifying crude sources and building reserves cushions India against Gulf attacks.
examples: Collapse of the 2022 Yemen truce
UN-brokered truce shattered by renewed Houthi–Saudi fighting since July
GS2 · West Asia / role of the UN
The breakdown of Yemen's 2022 truce shows the fragility of UN-brokered ceasefires.
pyqs: Energy security in foreign policy; Middle East.
Energy security and West Asia cooperation.

trend.t: West Asia questions repeatedly tie the region to India's energy security (2017, 2025); energy security was asked again in GS3 in 2026.
trend.watch: Energy security with a West Asia link was asked in 2017 and 2025, and in GS3 in 2026, so the current Gulf conflict is direct material.
focus: West Asia conflict and oil supply
Indian diaspora safety in the Gulf

potential: How does instability in West Asia threaten India's energy security? Suggest measures to reduce this vulnerability. (10 marks)

items.title: Safe harbour for social media platforms: Why Centre is weighing a legal rethink
items.syllabus: GS3 › Role of media and social networking sites in internal security challenges · GS2 › Government policies; regulation · GS2 › Fundamental rights (free speech)
items.summary: Explainer on the Centre's exploratory talks on whether social media platforms should keep 'safe harbour' under Section 79 of the IT Act; the IT Minister said platforms must take proactive steps on online harms.
evolution: Government looks at scrapping legal immunity for social media platforms (first safe harbour card).
IT Minister: platforms must take responsibility for child safety, women's safety and digital arrest.
Explained: why safe harbour matters and the options being explored.
ideas: What safe harbour is: Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 gives intermediaries conditional immunity for third-party content if they do not initiate, select the recipient of, or modify a transmission, and follow due diligence.
GS3 · Regulation of intermediaries
Section 79 shields platforms that act as neutral carriers and follow due diligence.

Not absolute: immunity is lost for involvement in unlawful activity or failure to act on lawful directions; Shreya Singhal (2015) tied takedowns under Section 79(3)(b) to a court order or government notification.
GS2 · Free speech / judiciary
Shreya Singhal ensured takedowns follow law, not private complaints, protecting free speech.
The core question: platforms use recommendation algorithms and their own community standards; can they still be called neutral intermediaries?
GS3 · Platform accountability
A platform that curates feeds with algorithms is more than a passive pipe.
Options and limits: confine safe harbour to passive services (ISPs, telecom, some messaging); any broad withdrawal would need IT Act amendments and Parliament's approval.
GS2 · Legislative process
Withdrawing safe harbour is a matter for Parliament, not an executive order.
keywords: Platforms boosting some content over others through recommendation systems
Algorithmic amplification weakens the claim that platforms are neutral carriers.
Duties intermediaries must meet to keep immunity
Safe harbour is earned through due diligence, not granted unconditionally.
A scam where fraudsters pose as officials and 'detain' victims over video calls
Digital arrest scams are one of the online harms the government wants platforms to tackle.
examples: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
Read down takedown obligations to court orders or government notifications
GS2 · Free speech / judicial review
Shreya Singhal shows the judiciary balancing platform regulation with free speech.
pyqs: Fake news and 2021 IT Rules amendments.
Social media and encrypted messaging threats.

trend.t: Social media questions moved from radicalisation (2015) to security threats from encrypted messaging (2024) and, in 2026, fake news and IT Rules amendments.
trend.watch: Platform regulation was asked in 2024 and 2026, so intermediary liability and safe harbour are the natural next step.
focus: Online harms: child safety, digital arrest

potential: Can platforms that use algorithms to amplify content still claim to be neutral intermediaries? Examine in the context of safe harbour under the IT Act. (10 marks)

items.title: AI has made Taiwan the world's fastest growing large economy
items.syllabus: GS3 › Growth and development; investment models · GS3 › Industrial policy (semiconductors) · GS3 › Science and technology (AI)
items.summary: Taiwan's GDP grew 14.36% in July–September 2026, driven by AI-linked investment and chip exports led by TSMC, overtaking India as the fastest growing large economy this year.
ideas: Investment-led boom: investments rose 26.36% year-on-year and accounted for almost half of Taiwan's 14.36% Q3 growth; investment and exports together explained almost 80%.
GS3 · Growth / investment
Taiwan's AI boom is investment-led: capital spending explains half its record growth.
One firm, one nation: TSMC, the world's largest chip manufacturer, was estimated to account for nearly a tenth of Taiwan's GDP; its 2026 revenue is seen at $175 billion, 43% higher.
GS3 · Semiconductors / industrial policy
TSMC alone is about a tenth of Taiwan's GDP, showing the value of owning a strategic technology.
Spillover: OCBC notes the AI upcycle is spilling from exports into local equipment spending and capacity expansion; South Korea and the US also posted strong AI-driven growth.
GS3 · Global value chains
The AI boom rewards economies that sit inside the hardware value chain.
For India: India's GDP grew 8.6% and 7.8% in the first two quarters of 2026; Indian markets were 'largely bypassed by the AI investment boom' (front page, p. 2).
GS3 · India's growth strategy
India grows fast on domestic demand, but Taiwan shows the premium of being in the AI hardware chain.
keywords: Growth driven by capital spending rather than consumption
Taiwan's 2026 surge is a textbook case of investment-led growth.
Dependence of an economy on one firm or sector
A tenth of GDP from one company brings growth and concentration risk.
data: Taiwan's Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics
Taiwan's GDP grew 14.36% in July–September 2026 on the back of AI investment.
examples: TSMC
World's largest chip maker, central to the global AI investment boom
GS3 · Semiconductor strategy
TSMC shows why India's Semiconductor Mission aims at chip making, not just assembly.

trend.t: Industrial policy questions moved from Make in India (2015) to manufacturing's share (2023) and, in 2025, PLI and the Semiconductor Mission.
trend.watch: Semiconductors and PLI were both asked in 2025, so comparative examples like Taiwan and South Korea are useful.
focus: Global value chains in AI hardware

potential: What lessons can India draw from Taiwan's semiconductor-led growth for its own industrial policy? (10 marks)

items.title: Seema Mitra award for BSF, SSB, cops from 2027; Rajnath pays tribute to war heroes at Sherathang
items.where: Nation, page 6 (Press Trust of India, Hingalganj and Gangtok)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Security challenges and their management in border areas · GS3 › Various security forces and their mandate · GS4 › Public service values (dedication, sacrifice)
items.summary: West Bengal will institute a 'Seema Mitra' award from 2027 for BSF, SSB and state police guarding borders, and promised more frontier police stations; Defence Minister Rajnath Singh paid tribute to war heroes near Nathu La.
ideas: Centre–state cooperation at the border: West Bengal shares over 2,200 km with Bangladesh; the state will facilitate more police stations in frontier areas with infrastructure, logistics and manpower.
GS3 · Border management
Border management needs state police and central forces working as one, as West Bengal's frontier police stations aim to do.
Morale and recognition: an award for exceptional contributions by BSF, SSB and state police acknowledges hard frontier duty.
GS3 · Security forces / GS4 · Motivation
Recognition like the Seema Mitra award sustains morale in forces guarding remote borders.
Sacrifice remembered: at the Sherathang war memorial on the India–China border, the Defence Minister said 'every generation of Indians will remember your sacrifice'.
GS4 · Public service values
War memorials keep alive the values of duty and sacrifice that public service rests on.
keywords: Coordinated work of central forces, state police and civil agencies at borders
Integrated border management joins central forces and state police in one system.
examples: BSF and SSB
BSF guards the India–Bangladesh border; SSB the borders with Nepal and Bhutan
GS3 · Security forces and their mandate
BSF and SSB show India's border-specific force design: one force, one frontier.
pyqs: China and Pakistan borders; BADP and BIM.

trend.t: Border questions moved from strategy (2016) and crimes across borders (2020) to specific programmes such as BADP and border infrastructure (2024, 2026).
trend.watch: Border infrastructure and development programmes were asked in 2024 and 2026, so Centre–state cooperation and force welfare are useful supporting points.
focus: Morale and welfare of border forces

potential: Discuss the role of state governments in managing India's international land borders. (10 marks)

ethics.title: Equity at the margins: the Siddis
ethics.news: A 15-year-old Siddi girl won India's Youth Olympics judo medal; her community, a PVTG of about 12,959 in Gujarat, gets ST status in Saurashtra but not outside it.
ethics.syllabus: Inclusive governance; equity; compassion towards the weaker sections
ethics.link: Inclusive governance is not equal treatment but equitable opportunity: coaching camps, education and consistent legal status for a tiny, historically enslaved community. The Siddi youth who drop out of sports camps show that access without support is incomplete inclusion.
ethics.question: "Inclusive governance is judged by how the state treats those at the margins." Discuss with an example of a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group.

ethics.title: After the guns: winning trust in Bastar
ethics.news: The PM said armed Naxals have been wiped out but 'intellectual Naxals' must be defeated; LWE districts have fallen to seven.
ethics.syllabus: Good governance; inclusive governance; balancing security and rights
ethics.link: Security operations restore order, but legitimacy comes from schools, roads, gram sabhas and respect for tribal rights. The ethical task now is to counter extremist ideas without treating dissent or tribal assertion as disloyalty.
ethics.question: "The end of armed insurgency is the beginning of a test of governance." Discuss the ethical responsibilities of administrators in areas freed from Left Wing Extremism.

ethics.title: When a population rule shuts women out
ethics.news: The SC said the two-child bar on panchayat office 'tended to weaken the position of women rather than empowering them'.
ethics.link: A rule neutral on paper can be unequal in effect: in a patriarchal society women have little control over family size, yet bear the disqualification. Inclusive governance means testing laws for their real effect on women, not their wording.
ethics.question: "Laws that are neutral in form can be discriminatory in effect." Illustrate with reference to women's participation in local governance.

ethics.title: Rights without rivalry
ethics.news: A petition seeks to stop recognising trans women as 'females'; the author urges debate that treats transgender persons as equal rights-bearers.
ethics.link: Equality is indivisible: one marginalised group's protection cannot be secured by excluding another. Empathy and reasoned debate, not fear, should guide how competing claims are balanced.
ethics.question: How can a public servant balance competing claims of two marginalised groups while upholding the constitutional value of equality?

ethics.title: A family knocking on every door
ethics.news: The family of a Raipur man detained in Russia has written to the CM, police, embassies and the PM's grievance portal for help.
ethics.syllabus: Citizen-centric governance; compassion towards the weaker sections; accountability
ethics.link: A file passing from police to state home department to MEA is due process; for a family whose son is detained abroad, it is anguish. Citizen-centric governance means a single point of contact, time-bound updates and compassion in communication.
ethics.question: "Due process without compassion becomes indifference." Examine with reference to citizens in distress abroad.

ethics.title: Rules made without asking
ethics.news: Maharashtra says FSSAI changed licence thresholds without public consultation and created central inspectors not provided in the Act.
ethics.syllabus: Good governance; transparency; rule of law
ethics.link: Even a well-intended rule loses legitimacy when made without consultation or beyond the law. The central official's worry, that a state's performance depends on one officer, is a lesson in building institutions that outlast individuals.
ethics.question: "Good governance rests on institutions, not individuals." Discuss with reference to regulatory enforcement.

ethics.title: Who pays for the warming?
ethics.news: The editorial notes that countries that contributed least to emissions, as the Nepal floods show, face the steepest costs.
ethics.link: Climate justice asks those who caused the problem to pay for its harms: finance for clean energy and a funded Loss and Damage Fund are moral obligations, not charity.
ethics.question: "Climate change is as much an ethical problem as a scientific one." Discuss with reference to loss and damage.

ethics.title: Dignity of mudwork
ethics.news: Young helpers in Kangra refused mudwork as 'dirty' and lowly, while cement work seemed modern and respectable; traditional masons are vanishing.
ethics.link: When society labels some work as low, it loses the skills and wisdom in it. Restoring dignity to traditional crafts, through pay, training and recognition, is both ethical and practical.
ethics.question: How do social attitudes towards certain kinds of work affect sustainable development? Discuss with examples.

ethics.title: Selling the lock and the key
ethics.news: AI firms that expose software vulnerabilities could also sell protection against them.
ethics.syllabus: Applied ethics: technology; conflict of interest
ethics.link: When the same company finds a flaw and sells its fix, incentives may favour exposure over safety. Responsible disclosure and transparency are ethical duties in dual-use technology.
ethics.question: Discuss the ethical concerns in the use of artificial intelligence in cyber security.

essay.title: The mud kitchen that breathes
essay.text: In Kangra, concrete rooms trap summer heat and become damp iceboxes in winter, while a traditional mud-and-slate kitchen stays cool in summer and warm in winter. The writer ends: 'Concrete doesn't bend.'
essay.use: For 'Forests precede civilizations and deserts follow them' (2024) and 'Nature is the symbol of the spirit' (2026).

essay.title: From a Kolhapur village to a boy band
essay.text: Darshan Magdum, 22, from Dundage village, began posting songs on Instagram as a hobby; a 'random call' brought him into the American boy band Boy Throb. His teacher parents took time to understand content creation, and still encouraged him to pursue a master's degree and a stable job.
essay.use: For 'Not all who wander are lost' (2023) and 'It is best to see life as a journey, not as a destination' (2025).

essay.title: Work as the democratic bargain
essay.text: Work gives people competence, independence, social standing and a stake in the future; the democratic bargain rests on the expectation that effort can improve one's circumstances.
essay.use: For 'Rise of Artificial Intelligence: the threat of jobless future...' (2019) and 'There can be no social justice without economic prosperity...' (2020).

essay.title: Teach to fish, not hand out fish
essay.text: On rationalising free food, the authors cite the adage that it is better to teach a person to catch fish than to hand out a free fish every day.
essay.use: For 'A society that has more justice is a society that needs less charity' (2023).

essay.title: Technology denial that built a nation
essay.text: Faced with restrictions on access to advanced technology, India's atomic energy programme built its own capabilities; scientific leadership, freedom for scientists, trust in young people and acceptance of failure made it possible.
essay.use: For 'The Empires of the future will be the empires of the mind' (2024) and 'Best lessons are learnt through bitter experiences' (2025).

essay.title: The grass that gets trampled
essay.text: A Raipur store manager who went to Russia for a job says he was jailed and pressured to join the Russian army in the war against Ukraine; his family, spending on lawyers, only wants him home.
essay.use: For 'When two elephants fight, it is the grass that gets trampled' (2026).
